claim: Chlamydomonas cells are approximately 10 μm in diameter.
source: Chlamydomonas cells are ∼10 μm in diameter, and about half of their volume is occupied by a single cup-shaped chloroplast (Figure 1A) (Sager and Palade, 1957; Gaffal et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the cell diameter measurement.

claim: About half of the volume of Chlamydomonas cells is occupied by a single cup-shaped chloroplast.
source: Chlamydomonas cells are ∼10 μm in diameter, and about half of their volume is occupied by a single cup-shaped chloroplast (Figure 1A) (Sager and Palade, 1957; Gaffal et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript states this proportion and references Figure 1A showing the chloroplast structure, supported by citations.

claim: Thylakoid stacks in Chlamydomonas have a lateral repeat distance of 22.4 ± 1.3 nm.
source: Thylakoid stacks had a lateral repeat distance of 22.4 ± 1.3 nm, with 4.9 ± 0.5 nm thylakoid membranes, 9.0 ± 1.4 nm thylakoid lumina, and 3.6 ± 0.5 nm interthylakoid stromal spaces (± denotes standard deviation, n = 38 thylakoids from eight stacks).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements with standard deviations and sample size.

claim: Chlamydomonas thylakoid membranes are 4.9 ± 0.5 nm thick.
source: Thylakoid stacks had a lateral repeat distance of 22.4 ± 1.3 nm, with 4.9 ± 0.5 nm thylakoid membranes, 9.0 ± 1.4 nm thylakoid lumina, and 3.6 ± 0.5 nm interthylakoid stromal spaces (± denotes standard deviation, n = 38 thylakoids from eight stacks).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements with standard deviations and sample size.

claim: Chlamydomonas thylakoid lumina are 9.0 ± 1.4 nm wide.
source: Thylakoid stacks had a lateral repeat distance of 22.4 ± 1.3 nm, with 4.9 ± 0.5 nm thylakoid membranes, 9.0 ± 1.4 nm thylakoid lumina, and 3.6 ± 0.5 nm interthylakoid stromal spaces (± denotes standard deviation, n = 38 thylakoids from eight stacks).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements with standard deviations and sample size.

claim: Interthylakoid stromal spaces in Chlamydomonas are 3.6 ± 0.5 nm wide.
source: Thylakoid stacks had a lateral repeat distance of 22.4 ± 1.3 nm, with 4.9 ± 0.5 nm thylakoid membranes, 9.0 ± 1.4 nm thylakoid lumina, and 3.6 ± 0.5 nm interthylakoid stromal spaces (± denotes standard deviation, n = 38 thylakoids from eight stacks).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific measurements with standard deviations and sample size.

claim: Chlamydomonas thylakoid lumina are significantly wider than thylakoid lumina in higher plant grana.
source: Although Chlamydomonas thylakoid lumina were significantly wider than the thylakoid lumina reported in studies of higher plant grana (15.7–16.3 nm lateral repeat, 4.5–4.7 nm thylakoid lumina, and 3.2–3.6 nm interthylakoid stromal spaces) (Daum et al., 2010; Kirchhoff et al., 2011), grana thylakoid lumina have been shown to expand to 9.2 nm when plants are adapted to light (Kirchhoff et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript compares measurements from this study with cited literature values.

claim: Higher plant grana have a lateral repeat distance of 15.7–16.3 nm.
source: Although Chlamydomonas thylakoid lumina were significantly wider than the thylakoid lumina reported in studies of higher plant grana (15.7–16.3 nm lateral repeat, 4.5–4.7 nm thylakoid lumina, and 3.2–3.6 nm interthylakoid stromal spaces) (Daum et al., 2010; Kirchhoff et al., 2011), grana thylakoid lumina have been shown to expand to 9.2 nm when plants are adapted to light (Kirchhoff et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature values for comparison.

claim: Grana thylakoid lumina expand to 9.2 nm when plants are adapted to light.
source: Although Chlamydomonas thylakoid lumina were significantly wider than the thylakoid lumina reported in studies of higher plant grana (15.7–16.3 nm lateral repeat, 4.5–4.7 nm thylakoid lumina, and 3.2–3.6 nm interthylakoid stromal spaces) (Daum et al., 2010; Kirchhoff et al., 2011), grana thylakoid lumina have been shown to expand to 9.2 nm when plants are adapted to light (Kirchhoff et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific finding from the literature.

claim: The number of thylakoids per stack in Chlamydomonas ranges from 2 to 15, with a median of 3.
source: In our tomograms, the number of thylakoids per stack ranged from 2 to 15, with a median of 3 thylakoids.
evidence: The manuscript reports the range and median from their tomogram data.

claim: Thylakoid lumina are less dense than the interthylakoid stromal space and the chloroplast stroma.
source: In agreement with previous reports from other organisms (Daum et al., 2010; Leforestier et al., 2012), thylakoid lumina were less dense than the interthylakoid stromal space and the chloroplast stroma (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation, references Figure 2 showing the density differences, and cites supporting literature.

claim: All thylakoids within the chloroplast form one continuous compartment.
source: It is thought that all of the thylakoids within the chloroplast form one continuous compartment (Mustárdy and Garab, 2003; Staehelin, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature proposing this structural organization.

claim: 3D visualization of thylakoid architecture revealed complex interconnected networks.
source: While our tomogram volumes were too confined to make a definitive assessment, 3D visualization of thylakoid architecture did indeed reveal complex interconnected networks (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from their 3D tomograms shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Thylakoid stacks frequently split along interthylakoid stromal spaces and merge with other stacks.
source: Thylakoid stacks frequently split along one or two of the interthylakoid stromal spaces, and the thylakoids on each side of these divisions continued and merged with other stacks (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 3B.

claim: Most thylakoid stacks are physically linked to each other.
source: In this manner, most thylakoid stacks were physically linked to each other.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from their observations of thylakoid splitting and merging.

claim: Thylakoid lumina are frequently continuous with each other where the tips of two adjacent thylakoids are conjoined by a 180° loop of the thylakoid membrane.
source: In addition to occasional thylakoid bifurcations and mergers, thylakoid lumina were most frequently continuous with each other where the tips of two adjacent thylakoids were conjoined by a 180° loop of the thylakoid membrane (most clearly seen in Figures 3A and 4F).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing specific figures.

claim: Fenestrations in Chlamydomonas thylakoids often perforate entire stacks and may allow free diffusion of the chloroplast stroma.
source: Like the photosynthetic membranes of cyanobacteria (Nevo et al., 2007; Ting et al., 2007), we observed fenestrations in Chlamydomonas thylakoids that often perforated entire stacks and may allow free diffusion of the chloroplast stroma (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from their tomograms and speculates on function, with citations to similar structures in cyanobacteria.

claim: At thylakoid tip convergence zones, the double membrane structure of the chloroplast envelope appeared to lose definition.
source: At these thylakoid tip convergence zones (Figure 3C–F and 4C–F), the double membrane structure of the chloroplast envelope appeared to lose definition and in some spots was reduced to a single dense plane without an intermembrane space (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing specific figures.

claim: Thylakoid tip convergence zones contain chloroplast envelope invaginations and small vesicles between the chloroplast envelope and thylakoid tips.
source: These regions also contained chloroplast envelope invaginations (Figure 3C) and small vesicles between the chloroplast envelope and thylakoid tips (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing specific figures.

claim: Thylakoid tip convergence zones are always present at the apical rim of the chloroplast cup.
source: Thylakoid tip convergence zones were always present at the apical rim of the chloroplast cup (Figure 4), but they were also found near the base of the cup (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the locations where these structures were observed in their tomograms.

claim: Invaginations protrude from the chloroplast envelope inner membrane into the stroma.
source: In nearly every tomogram, we noticed invaginations that protruded from the chloroplast envelope inner membrane into the stroma (Figures 3, 4, 6 and 7).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing multiple figures.

claim: The median density of invaginations on the chloroplast envelope inner membrane is 12/μm².
source: The density of invaginations on the membrane varied widely, with a median of 12/μm2 (Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript reports a quantitative measurement from their data, shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Invaginations are especially prevalent near thylakoid tip convergence zones and at the base-lobe junction.
source: However, we did note that invaginations were especially prevalent near thylakoid tip convergence zones and at the base-lobe junction (Figure 7), where the base and the sides of the chloroplast cup meet.
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 7.

claim: 34% of invaginations are positioned less than 40 nm from a thylakoid tip.
source: In our dataset, 34% of the invaginations were positioned less than 40 nm from a thylakoid tip, and 64% were found within 100 nm of a tip (Figure 8D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements from their data, shown in Figure 8D.

claim: 64% of invaginations are found within 100 nm of a thylakoid tip.
source: In our dataset, 34% of the invaginations were positioned less than 40 nm from a thylakoid tip, and 64% were found within 100 nm of a tip (Figure 8D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative measurements from their data, shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Inner membrane invaginations may provide a route for the exchange of lipids and proteins between the chloroplast envelope and thylakoid compartments.
source: Thus, inner membrane invaginations may provide a route for the exchange of lipids and proteins between the chloroplast envelope and thylakoid compartments.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this function based on the proximity of invaginations to thylakoid tips.

claim: Direct connections between thylakoid tips and the chloroplast envelope inner membrane were observed.
source: Indeed, we observed a few direct connections between thylakoid tips and the chloroplast envelope inner membrane (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 6E-H.

claim: Direct connections between thylakoid tips and the chloroplast envelope inner membrane are rare.
source: These connections were rare, which could help maintain the distinct identities of each membrane and preserve the high proton concentration within the thylakoids.
evidence: The manuscript describes the frequency of these connections and speculates on their functional significance.

claim: The cluster of RuBisCO complexes in the pyrenoid is encased in a starch sheath.
source: The cluster of RuBisCO complexes in the pyrenoid was encased in a starch sheath (Figures 1G, 3A–B and 9A–B), and non-spherical starch granules were found throughout the chloroplast (Figures 1G, 3A–B, 4A–B and 7A–B).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing multiple figures.

claim: Non-spherical starch granules are found throughout the chloroplast.
source: The cluster of RuBisCO complexes in the pyrenoid was encased in a starch sheath (Figures 1G, 3A–B and 9A–B), and non-spherical starch granules were found throughout the chloroplast (Figures 1G, 3A–B, 4A–B and 7A–B).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing multiple figures.

claim: Plastoglobules are 64 ± 15 nm spherical structures.
source: In addition to starch, we observed smaller 64 ± 15 nm spherical plastoglobules (n = 20 globules from 9 tomograms) (Greenwood et al., 1963; Ohad et al., 1967b) that were always closely associated with thylakoid membranes (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from their data with sample size, referencing Figure 4 and citing literature.

claim: Plastoglobules are always closely associated with thylakoid membranes.
source: In addition to starch, we observed smaller 64 ± 15 nm spherical plastoglobules (n = 20 globules from 9 tomograms) (Greenwood et al., 1963; Ohad et al., 1967b) that were always closely associated with thylakoid membranes (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 4.

claim: Higher plant plastoglobules share a half-lipid bilayer with thylakoid membranes.
source: Higher plant plastoglobules were previously shown by freeze-fracture to share a half-lipid bilayer with thylakoid membranes (Austin et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific finding from the literature about higher plant plastoglobules.

claim: Chlamydomonas plastoglobules appear to be discontinuous from thylakoid membranes.
source: Given the caveat that the resolution of our CCD-acquired tomograms did not reveal the two layers of lipid bilayers, Chlamydomonas plastoglobules appeared to be discontinuous from thylakoid membranes, although punctate contacts were sometimes observed (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms with a caveat about resolution, referencing Figure 4A,D.

claim: Chlamydomonas plastoglobules are primarily found adjacent to flat thylakoid sheets.
source: Additionally, while higher plant plastoglobules are frequently localized to areas of high membrane curvature, where they are proposed to form (Austin et al., 2006), Chlamydomonas plastoglobules were primarily found adjacent to flat thylakoid sheets (Figures 4, 7A–B and 9A).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, contrasting with cited literature on higher plants.

claim: Chlamydomonas plastoglobules are believed to contain lipids and thylakoid components similar to the plastoglobules of higher plants.
source: Although the composition of Chlamydomonas plastoglobules is currently unknown (Goodson et al., 2011), they are believed to contain lipids and thylakoid components similar to the plastoglobules of higher plants (Steinmüller and Tevini, 1985; Ytterberg et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature proposing compositional similarity to higher plant plastoglobules.

claim: Chlamydomonas plastoglobule structure remains intact at electron doses that damage starch granules.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, Chlamydomonas plastoglobule structure remained intact at electron doses that did not affect lipid membranes but damaged the radiation-sensitive starch granules (seen by bubbling within the granules, Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from their tomograms showing differential radiation sensitivity, referencing Figure 4A.

claim: Membrane tubules extend from the thylakoids into the pyrenoid through fenestrations in the starch sheath.
source: Membrane tubules extend from the thylakoids into the pyrenoid through fenestrations in the starch sheath (Sager and Palade, 1957; Ohad et al., 1967b).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing these structures.

claim: Pyrenoid tubules have a mean diameter of 107 ± 26 nm.
source: Thylakoid stacks often changed direction (Figure 9A–D) as their sheets merged with each other and narrowed into cylindrical pyrenoid tubules (Figure 10), which had a mean diameter of 107 ± 26 nm (n = 46 tubules from 10 tomograms).
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from their data with sample size, referencing figures.

claim: A 5–10 nm RuBisCO-free space is frequently observed surrounding pyrenoid tubules.
source: A 5–10 nm RuBisCO-free space was frequently observed surrounding the tubules (Figure 9E,G).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 9E,G.

claim: Deeper within the pyrenoid, pyrenoid tubules begin to twist and sometimes abruptly change direction by >90°.
source: Deeper within the pyrenoid, pyrenoid tubules began to twist (Figure 9A, top tubule), sometimes abruptly changed direction by >90° (Figure 9B, bottom tubule), and eventually lost their cylindrical structure as the tubules converged at the pyrenoid center, forming elaborate interconnected networks of variably shaped smaller membranes (Figure 9B).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing specific figures.

claim: Pyrenoid tubules eventually lose their cylindrical structure and form interconnected networks at the pyrenoid center.
source: Deeper within the pyrenoid, pyrenoid tubules began to twist (Figure 9A, top tubule), sometimes abruptly changed direction by >90° (Figure 9B, bottom tubule), and eventually lost their cylindrical structure as the tubules converged at the pyrenoid center, forming elaborate interconnected networks of variably shaped smaller membranes (Figure 9B).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 9B.

claim: Pyrenoid tubules contain smaller tubules termed pyrenoid minitubules.
source: Interestingly, in high magnification cryo-tomograms these structures were revealed to be smaller tubules (Figure 9E–H and Figure 9—figure supplement 1), which we have termed pyrenoid minitubules.
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing specific figures.

claim: Each pyrenoid tubule encompasses between two and eight minitubules, with a median of 5.
source: Each pyrenoid tubule encompassed between two and eight minitubules, with a median of 5.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative observations from their data.

claim: Pyrenoid minitubules have a long-axis diameter of 21.6 ± 1.7 nm and a short-axis diameter of 13.4 ± 1.1 nm in cross-section.
source: In cross-section, the minitubules had an oval or bean-like shape (Figure 9E,G) with a long-axis diameter of 21.6 ± 1.7 nm and a short-axis diameter of 13.4 ± 1.1 nm, including the membrane (n = 22 minitubules within four pyrenoid tubules).
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from their data with sample size, referencing figures.

claim: Pyrenoid minitubules enclose hollow lumina that are 3.5 ± 0.5 nm wide along the short-axis.
source: The minitubules enclosed hollow lumina that were 3.5 ± 0.5 nm wide along the short-axis, comparable in width to the interthylakoid stromal space.
evidence: The manuscript reports measurements from their data and makes a comparison.

claim: The lumina of pyrenoid tubules are continuous with the lumina of thylakoids.
source: Segmentation of the stack-to-tubule transition showed that the lumina of pyrenoid tubules were continuous with the lumina of thylakoids, while the lumina of pyrenoid minitubules were continuous with the stroma in the interthylakoid space (Figure 10).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their segmentation analysis, referencing Figure 10.

claim: The lumina of pyrenoid minitubules are continuous with the stroma in the interthylakoid space.
source: Segmentation of the stack-to-tubule transition showed that the lumina of pyrenoid tubules were continuous with the lumina of thylakoids, while the lumina of pyrenoid minitubules were continuous with the stroma in the interthylakoid space (Figure 10).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their segmentation analysis, referencing Figure 10.

claim: Minitubule membranes are derived from the coalescence of two opposed membranes of adjacent thylakoids in a stack.
source: Minitubule membranes were derived from the coalescence of two opposed membranes of adjacent thylakoids in a stack (Figure 10C–F).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their segmentation analysis, referencing Figure 10C-F.

claim: Minitubule membrane topology is 'inside-out' relative to the membranes of pyrenoid tubules.
source: Consequently, minitubule membrane topology is 'inside-out' relative to the membranes of pyrenoid tubules.
evidence: The manuscript infers this topological relationship from their structural observations.

claim: At the periphery of the pyrenoid, minitubules are completely enveloped within the surrounding pyrenoid tubule membrane.
source: At the periphery of the pyrenoid, minitubules were completely enveloped within the surrounding pyrenoid tubule membrane (Figure 9E–H).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 9E-H.

claim: As pyrenoid tubules proceed towards the center of the pyrenoid, minitubules emerge from the pyrenoid tubules, exposing their stromal lumina to the pyrenoid matrix.
source: As pyrenoid tubules proceeded towards the center of the pyrenoid, minitubules emerged from the pyrenoid tubules, exposing their stromal lumina to the pyrenoid matrix (Figure 11A–E).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 11A-E.

claim: RuBisCO accounts for over 90% of the pyrenoid's protein content.
source: RuBisCO accounts for over 90% of the pyrenoid's protein content (Holdsworth, 1971).
evidence: The manuscript cites a specific finding from the literature.

claim: Crystalline packing of RuBisCO complexes has been described in a few algal pyrenoids.
source: Such homogeneity suggests that the pyrenoid may exhibit higher-order organization, and indeed, 'crystalline' packing of RuBisCO complexes has been described in a few algal pyrenoids (Holdsworth, 1968; Kowallik, 1969) as well as bacterial carboxysomes (Schmid et al., 2006; Iancu et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing crystalline packing in some species.

claim: The pyrenoids of most species, including Chlamydomonas, appear amorphous.
source: However, the pyrenoids of most species, including those found in Chlamydomonas, appear amorphous (Griffiths, 1970; Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing the appearance of Chlamydomonas pyrenoids.

claim: Subtomogram averaging revealed that RuBisCO complexes in the Chlamydomonas pyrenoid are hexagonally packed.
source: However, symmetry-free subtomogram averaging of 45.6 nm3 subvolumes revealed that the RuBisCO complexes were actually hexagonally packed (Figure 12B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of their subtomogram averaging analysis, referencing Figure 12B.

claim: The subtomogram average of RuBisCO complexes shows the A-B-A layered arrangement characteristic of hexagonal close packing.
source: Furthermore, the average clearly showed the A-B-A layered arrangement of complexes that is a hallmark of hexagonal close packing (Figure 12B, bottom right).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural features observed in their subtomogram average, referencing Figure 12B.

claim: Hexagonal close packing has a smaller RMSD from the RuBisCO nearest neighbor positions than cubic close packing or body-centered cubic packing.
source: We generated ideal hard sphere models and found that hexagonal close packing had a smaller root-mean-squared deviation (RMSD) from our point cloud center positions than cubic close packing or body-centered cubic packing (Figure 12D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of their modeling analysis, referencing Figure 12D.

claim: RuBisCO complexes within the pyrenoid have approximately 15 nm between their centers.
source: Additionally, hexagonal close packing with a spherical diameter of 15.05 nm yielded a unique minimum RMSD, indicating that RuBisCO complexes within the pyrenoid have ∼15 nm between their centers (Figure 12D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the results of their modeling analysis, referencing Figure 12D.

claim: RuBisCO complexes positioned 15 nm apart have a 2–4.5 nm space between their surfaces.
source: Given the dimensions of RuBisCO, complexes positioned 15 nm apart would have a 2–4.5 nm space between their surfaces (Figure 12E).
evidence: The manuscript calculates this spacing based on known RuBisCO dimensions and their measured center-to-center distance, referencing Figure 12E.

claim: Eyespot globules are similar in appearance to plastoglobules but slightly larger.
source: Viewed by cryo-ET, the eyespot globules were similar in appearance to plastoglobules dispersed throughout the chloroplast (Figure 14A), although they were slightly larger (Figure 14G) and densely packed along two adjacent thylakoid membranes.
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figures 14A and 14G.

claim: Eyespot globules are densely packed along two adjacent thylakoid membranes.
source: Viewed by cryo-ET, the eyespot globules were similar in appearance to plastoglobules dispersed throughout the chloroplast (Figure 14A), although they were slightly larger (Figure 14G) and densely packed along two adjacent thylakoid membranes.
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 14A.

claim: The two arrays of eyespot globules, the associated thylakoids, and the bordering chloroplast envelope are all slightly concave relative to the plasma membrane.
source: The two arrays of eyespot globules, the associated thylakoids, and the bordering chloroplast envelope were all slightly concave relative to the plasma membrane (Figure 14B).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 14B.

claim: Eyespot curvature may be variable.
source: However, Chlamydomonas eyespots with straight or convex globule arrays have frequently been observed in plastic section TEM images (Kreimer, 2009), indicating that eyespot curvature may be variable.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature showing different eyespot morphologies and infers variability.

claim: Eyespot globules are proposed to reflect incident light back to channelrhodopsin photoreceptors in the plasma membrane while absorbing light from other directions.
source: The eyespot globules are proposed to reflect incident light coming from outside the cell back to channelrhodopsin photoreceptors in the overlying plasma membrane, while simultaneously absorbing light passing through the cell from other directions (Foster and Smyth, 1980; Kreimer and Melkonian, 1990).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature proposing this functional mechanism.

claim: Concave eyespot architecture may enhance reflection by focusing reflected light.
source: Concave eyespot architecture may enhance reflection, as it has been shown to focus reflected light in a different species of green algae (Kreimer and Melkonian, 1990).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature showing this effect in another species and speculates on its relevance.

claim: A cluster of unilamellar and bilamellar vesicles is embedded between the cell wall and the rhodopsin-containing region of the plasma membrane adjacent to the eyespot.
source: We observed a cluster of unilamellar and bilamellar vesicles embedded between the cell wall and the rhodopsin-containing region of the plasma membrane (Figure 14D–F).
evidence: The manuscript describes structural observations from their tomograms, referencing Figure 14D-F.

claim: Vesicles adjacent to the eyespot have not been previously described.
source: To our knowledge, such structures have not been previously described, although voids in the cell wall near the eyespot have been seen in conventional plastic sections (G Kreimer and S Geimer, personal communication, May 2014).
evidence: The manuscript states this is a novel observation, with a personal communication noting related observations.

claim: Vesicles adjacent to the eyespot were only observed adjacent to the eyespot apparatus, implying they may be related to eyespot function.
source: Comparing all of our tomograms containing the cell wall, these vesicles were only observed adjacent to the eyespot apparatus, implying that they may be related to eyespot function.
evidence: The manuscript infers a functional relationship based on the specific localization of these vesicles.

claim: The Chlamydomonas interthylakoid stromal space is comparable to the grana interthylakoid stromal space.
source: The Chlamydomonas interthylakoid stromal space (3.6 nm) is comparable to the grana interthylakoid stromal space (3.2–3.6 nm) (Daum et al., 2010; Kirchhoff et al., 2011), indicating that the molecular mechanisms that hold two algal or higher plant thylakoid membranes together may be similar.
evidence: The manuscript compares their measurements with cited literature values and infers mechanistic similarity.

claim: The attraction between thylakoid membranes is proposed to involve van der Waals and electrostatic interactions between membrane surfaces.
source: This attraction is proposed to involve van der Waals and electrostatic interactions between membrane surfaces (Barber and Chow, 1979; Chow et al., 2005), perhaps mediated by light-harvesting complexes bound to photosystem II (PSII) (Daum et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature proposing these molecular mechanisms.

claim: The oxygen-evolving complex of PSII projects 4.5 nm into the thylakoid lumen.
source: The oxygen-evolving complex (OEC) of PSII projects 4.5 nm into the thylakoid lumen (Ferreira et al., 2004), a comparable distance to the 4.5–4.7 nm width of grana thylakoid lumina measured for isolated chloroplasts and leaves of dark-adapted plants (Daum et al., 2010; Kirchhoff et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature values for the OEC projection distance and compares with grana lumen widths.

claim: OECs on opposite sides of narrow grana lumina must interdigitate due to spatial constraints.
source: Thus, OECs on opposite sides of these narrow lumina must interdigitate due to spatial constraints (Daum et al., 2010), and indeed, it seems likely that the size of the OEC determines the minimum grana lumen width.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and infers this structural constraint.

claim: PSII complexes in Chlamydomonas thylakoids and light-exposed higher plant grana should experience fewer limitations to their mobility.
source: Thus, PSII complexes in Chlamydomonas thylakoids and light-exposed higher plant grana should experience fewer limitations to their mobility, and their OECs may directly face each other instead of being interdigitated.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the wider lumen spacing observed in their data and cited literature.

claim: CURT1 is a candidate protein for organizing the 180° loops between thylakoid tips.
source: One good candidate for the 180° loops is CURT1, an evolutionarily conserved family of proteins that oligomerize, tubulate membranes, and are enriched at the grana margins of higher plants (Armbruster et al., 2013; Pribil et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing CURT1 properties and speculates on its role.

claim: Thylakoids have a similar lipid composition to the chloroplast envelope inner membrane.
source: While the thylakoid and chloroplast envelope membranes are widely believed to be independent systems, thylakoids have a similar lipid composition to the chloroplast envelope inner membrane (Kelly and Dormann, 2004) and require the import of proteins encoded by the nuclear genome (Green, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing lipid composition and protein import requirements.

claim: There is growing evidence that vesicular transport from the chloroplast envelope inner membrane is required for thylakoid biogenesis.
source: Consistent with this idea, there is growing evidence that vesicular transport from the chloroplast envelope inner membrane is required for thylakoid biogenesis (Kroll et al., 2001; Garcia et al., 2010; Nordhues et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting this mechanism.

claim: Chlamydomonas thylakoid biogenesis may be spatially regulated.
source: Recent work suggests that Chlamydomonas thylakoid biogenesis may be spatially regulated (Uniacke and Zerges, 2009; Schottkowski et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature proposing spatial regulation.

claim: Thylakoid proteins encoded by the chloroplast genome are locally translated at the base of the chloroplast cup in the T-zone.
source: In the model proposed by these studies, thylakoid proteins encoded by the chloroplast genome are locally translated at the base of the chloroplast cup in a region surrounding the pyrenoid called the T-zone (Uniacke and Zerges, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature proposing this model of spatial organization.

claim: At the base-lobe junction, nuclear-encoded proteins are imported and assembled with chloroplast-encoded proteins into macromolecular complexes in the thylakoid membranes.
source: At the base-lobe junction, where the base and sides of the cup meet, nuclear-encoded proteins are imported and assembled with the chloroplast-encoded proteins into macromolecular complexes in the thylakoid membranes.
evidence: The manuscript describes a model from cited literature.

claim: Mature thylakoids in the sides of the chloroplast cup carry out the photosynthetic light reactions.
source: Finally, mature thylakoids in the sides of the cup carry out the photosynthetic light reactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes a model from cited literature.

claim: Small complexes observed at the base-lobe junction may be undergoing import.
source: Indeed, in this junction region we observed small complexes associated with both the chloroplast envelope outer membrane and inner membrane invaginations, indicating that these complexes may be undergoing import (Figure 7).
evidence: The manuscript describes observations from their tomograms and speculates on function, referencing Figure 7.

claim: The rim of the chloroplast cup could be the site where old and photodamaged thylakoid proteins are transported out for degradation.
source: One possibility is that the rim could be the site where old and photodamaged thylakoid proteins are transported out of the chloroplast for degradation.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this as a speculative possibility.

claim: Thylakoid tip convergence zones may be a conserved feature of algal chloroplasts.
source: It is possible that thylakoid tip convergence zones are a conserved feature of algal chloroplasts, as similar structures can be found in a wide range of algae (Gibbs, 1962; Moisan et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature showing similar structures in other algae and speculates on conservation.

claim: Thylakoid tip convergence zones may be homologous to the biogenesis centers of cyanobacteria.
source: Furthermore, thylakoid tip convergence zones may be homologous to the biogenesis centers of cyanobacteria (Kunkel, 1982; van de Meene et al., 2006; Stengel et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature on cyanobacterial structures and speculates on homology.

claim: RuBisCO activase is localized to the pyrenoid and requires ATP to promote RuBisCO activity.
source: However, RuBisCO activase is also localized to the pyrenoid (McKay and Gibbs, 1991) and requires ATP to promote RuBisCO activity (Streusand and Portis, 1987).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing RuBisCO activase localization and function.

claim: Phosphoribulokinase has been detected in close association with the pyrenoid.
source: While immunolabeling data indicates that many Calvin–Benson cycle enzymes may be restricted to the stroma (Suss et al., 1995), phosphoribulokinase (PRK), which uses ATP to carry out the final step of ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) regeneration, has been detected in close association with the pyrenoid (Holdsworth, 1971; McKay and Gibbs, 1991).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing PRK localization.

claim: The pyrenoid likely requires ATP from the chloroplast stroma.
source: Thus, the pyrenoid likely requires ATP from the chloroplast stroma.
evidence: The manuscript infers this requirement based on the localization of ATP-requiring enzymes in the pyrenoid.

claim: The product of carbon fixation, G3P, must be exported from the pyrenoid.
source: Conversely, the product of carbon fixation, G3P, must be exported from the pyrenoid.
evidence: The manuscript infers this necessity based on the spatial separation of carbon fixation and downstream metabolism.

claim: Pyrenoid minitubules facilitate the rapid targeted diffusion of small molecules such as ATP and Calvin-Benson cycle sugars between the interthylakoid stromal space and the pyrenoid matrix.
source: Therefore, we propose that minitubules facilitate the rapid targeted diffusion of small molecules such as ATP and Calvin–Benson cycle sugars between these two compartments.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this function based on the structural connectivity and dimensions of minitubules.

claim: Diffusion through minitubules would be practically one-dimensional.
source: The minitubule lumen diameter is only 3–4 nm by 8–15 nm, while the longest axes of ATP and the sugars RuBP and G3P measure ∼1.4 nm, ∼1.2 nm, and ∼0.7 nm, respectively. Thus, diffusion of these metabolites through the minitubules would be practically one-dimensional.
evidence: The manuscript compares the dimensions of minitubule lumina with molecular dimensions and infers the nature of diffusion.

claim: It would take only a few milliseconds for a small molecule to travel 1 μm through a minitubule.
source: While we are unsure how the local minitubule environment may affect the diffusion coefficient, assuming a diffusion coefficient of a small molecule in the cytoplasm (Milo et al., 2010), it would only take a few milliseconds to travel 1 μm through a minitubule.
evidence: The manuscript calculates this diffusion time based on cited diffusion coefficients.

claim: HCO3− in the thylakoid lumen is converted to CO2 by carbonic anhydrase 3 (CAH3).
source: It is believed that HCO3− in the thylakoid lumen is converted to CO2 by carbonic anhydrase 3 (CAH3) (Karlsson et al., 1998; Hanson et al., 2003), a reaction that is aided by the high H+ concentration in the lumen (Raven, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing this enzymatic reaction.

claim: Membranes are much more permeable to CO2 than HCO3−.
source: Since membranes are much more permeable to CO2 than HCO3− (Moroney et al., 2011), CO2 would then freely diffuse out of the thylakoids and into the pyrenoid.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing membrane permeability and infers diffusion behavior.

claim: Under low-CO2 conditions, CAH3 moves from the thylakoids to the pyrenoid tubules.
source: Under low-CO2 conditions, CAH3 is phosphorylated and moves from the thylakoids to the pyrenoid tubules, where it can efficiently supply RuBisCO with CO2 (Blanco-Rivero et al., 2012; Sinetova et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing CAH3 relocalization under specific conditions.

claim: The structure of the pyrenoid is dynamic and responds to environmental changes including light, temperature, and atmospheric composition.
source: The structure of the pyrenoid is dynamic and responds to environmental changes including light, temperature, and atmospheric composition.
evidence: The manuscript states this general property of pyrenoid structure.

claim: When cells are grown in low light, the pyrenoid matrix becomes fenestrated with more pyrenoid tubules.
source: When cells are grown in low light, the pyrenoid matrix becomes fenestrated with more pyrenoid tubules (Rawat et al., 1996).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing this structural response to light conditions.

claim: The hexagonal arrangement of RuBisCO complexes could be caused by specific interactions between complexes or by non-specific packing forces.
source: The hexagonal arrangement of RuBisCO complexes within the pyrenoid could be caused by one of two distinct influences. Either there are specific interactions between RuBisCO complexes that enforce this hexagonal configuration, or non-specific packing forces resulting from crowding within the pyrenoid compress the complexes together, yielding hexagonal close packing of roughly spherical objects.
evidence: The manuscript proposes two alternative explanations for the observed packing.

claim: Hydrophobic residues in the surface-exposed α-helixes of the RuBisCO small subunit are necessary for pyrenoid formation.
source: The hydrophobic residues in the surface-exposed α-helixes of the RuBisCO small subunit were shown to be necessary for pyrenoid formation, and RuBisCO aggregation was prevented in vivo when these domains were replaced by less hydrophobic sequences from higher plants.
evidence: The manuscript cites findings from literature about the role of specific residues.

claim: Hydrophobic interactions between RuBisCO complexes may drive pyrenoid formation.
source: This implies that hydrophobic interactions between RuBisCO complexes may drive pyrenoid formation.
evidence: The manuscript infers this mechanism from cited experimental results.

claim: There is a 2–4.5 nm space between RuBisCO complexes in the pyrenoid, suggesting they may not directly interact.
source: We found that the centers of RuBisCO complexes in the pyrenoid were ∼15 nm apart (Figure 12D), even though RuBisCO is shaped like a rounded cube with a shortest diameter of ∼10.5 nm and a longest diameter of ∼13 nm. Thus, there is a 2–4.5 nm space between RuBisCO complexes, depending on their relative orientations (Figure 12E). This data suggests that RuBisCO complexes within the pyrenoid may not directly interact with each other and that other factors, such as a dense matrix of proteins and carbohydrates or small linker proteins between the complexes (Meyer and Griffiths, 2013), determine the RuBisCO spacing.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from their measurements and molecular dimensions, referencing figures and citing literature.

claim: In α-carboxysomes, non-specific packing forces alone are believed to be sufficient to induce the layered organization of RuBisCO.
source: In α-carboxysomes, which are found primarily in ocean-dwelling cyanobacteria, non-specific packing forces alone are believed to be sufficient to induce the layered organization of RuBisCO (Iancu et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing RuBisCO organization in α-carboxysomes.

claim: In β-carboxysomes, RuBisCO complexes are held in an organized array by CcmM linker proteins.
source: However, in the β-carboxysomes of freshwater cyanobacteria, RuBisCO complexes are held in an organized array by CcmM linker proteins (Long et al., 2007, 2010; Peña et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing RuBisCO organization in β-carboxysomes.

claim: The pyrenoid forms in mutants that lack a starch sheath.
source: Additionally, the pyrenoid forms in mutants that lack a starch sheath (Villarejo et al., 1996), enabling a direct test of whether the starch induces hexagonal packing of RuBisCO.
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing mutant phenotypes and proposes an experimental approach.

claim: Cryo-FIB combined with cryo-ET was used to acquire the first in situ 3D structures of the algal chloroplast.
source: By combining cryo-focused ion beam milling of vitreous Chlamydomonas cells with cryo-electron tomography, we acquired three-dimensional structures of the chloroplast in its native state within the cell.
evidence: The manuscript states this methodological achievement in the abstract.

claim: Chloroplast envelope inner membrane invaginations were frequently found in close association with thylakoid tips.
source: Chloroplast envelope inner membrane invaginations were frequently found in close association with thylakoid tips, and the tips of multiple thylakoid stacks converged at dynamic sites on the chloroplast envelope, implicating lipid transport in thylakoid biogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation from the abstract and implies functional significance.

claim: The tips of multiple thylakoid stacks converge at dynamic sites on the chloroplast envelope, implicating lipid transport in thylakoid biogenesis.

claim: Thylakoid stacks and the pyrenoid are connected by cylindrical pyrenoid tubules.

claim: Multiple parallel minitubules are bundled within each pyrenoid tubule.

evidence: The manuscript states this structural observation from the abstract and speculates on function.

claim: Minitubules possibly serve as conduits for the targeted one-dimensional diffusion of small molecules such as ATP and sugars between the chloroplast stroma and the pyrenoid matrix.

claim: The chloroplast is the site of eukaryotic photosynthesis and carbon fixation.
source: The chloroplast is the site of eukaryotic photosynthesis and carbon fixation, coupled processes that convert the energy of light into stored biochemical energy, while exchanging environmental CO2 for O2.
evidence: The manuscript states this fundamental biological knowledge.

claim: The chloroplast directly and indirectly sustains much of the life on our planet.
source: As such, the chloroplast both directly and indirectly sustains much of the life on our planet.
evidence: The manuscript states this based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: In both higher plants and algae, the light-dependent photosynthetic reactions take place in the thylakoids.
source: In both higher plants and algae, the light-dependent photosynthetic reactions take place in the thylakoids, sheet-like membrane-bound compartments that group together into regularly-spaced stacks (called grana in higher plants).
evidence: The manuscript states this established biological knowledge.

claim: Thylakoids are sheet-like membrane-bound compartments that group together into regularly-spaced stacks.
source: In both higher plants and algae, the light-dependent photosynthetic reactions take place in the thylakoids, sheet-like membrane-bound compartments that group together into regularly-spaced stacks (called grana in higher plants).

claim: Photons are absorbed by photosystem complexes within the thylakoid membrane.
source: Photons are absorbed by photosystem complexes within the thylakoid membrane, and the downstream electron transfer chain generates NADPH in the chloroplast stroma.
evidence: The manuscript states this established biological knowledge.

claim: The electron transfer chain generates NADPH in the chloroplast stroma.
source: Photons are absorbed by photosystem complexes within the thylakoid membrane, and the downstream electron transfer chain generates NADPH in the chloroplast stroma.
evidence: The manuscript states this established biological knowledge.

claim: The splitting of H2O into O2 and H+ concentrates H+ inside the thylakoid lumen.
source: This process, combined with the splitting of H20 into O2 and H+, concentrates H+ inside the thylakoid lumen.
evidence: The manuscript states this established biological knowledge.

claim: The proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane is used by ATP synthase to generate ATP in the chloroplast stroma.
source: The resulting proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane is used by the ATP synthase complex to generate ATP in the chloroplast stroma, where the light-independent carbon fixation reactions occur.
evidence: The manuscript states this established biological knowledge.

claim: ATP and NADPH power the Calvin-Benson cycle.

claim: The majority of algal RuBisCO complexes are concentrated in the pyrenoid.
source: In order to maintain efficient carbon fixation, the majority of algal RuBisCO complexes are concentrated in a specialized region of the chloroplast known as the pyrenoid (Holdsworth, 1971; Lacoste-Royal and Gibbs, 1987; Borkhsenious et al., 1998), where carbonic anhydrase frees CO2 from solution (Karlsson et al., 1998; Moroney et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing this algal adaptation.

claim: Carbonic anhydrase in the pyrenoid frees CO2 from solution.
source: In order to maintain efficient carbon fixation, the majority of algal RuBisCO complexes are concentrated in a specialized region of the chloroplast known as the pyrenoid (Holdsworth, 1971; Lacoste-Royal and Gibbs, 1987; Borkhsenious et al., 1998), where carbonic anhydrase frees CO2 from solution (Karlsson et al., 1998; Moroney et al., 2011).
